cells.tense: You are the one who sees the whole pattern, and you are still in it.
cells.ask: Take one arrangement that feels uneven with someone close. Say what you see and ask what they see. Let their answer change one number, then leave it.
cells.core:
You see the pattern whole and you don't close the book on it. That's the thing most people lose first when they get good at seeing. They start finishing other people's sentences and call it insight.

You stay in the room with what you haven't finished knowing. The picture keeps taking on detail. That isn't indecision, it's how knowing stays honest. What keeps this from hardening into a pronouncement you'd have to defend is contact — recognition that doesn't swallow the person you're looking at, or you. What this balance is free to feed next is the kind of exchange where both people get their bearings back, not just the one being seen.
cells.sheetLine: You see it whole and you keep it open.
cells.verb: seeing the whole pattern, from inside it and outside it at once
cells.place: where fair balance between people is settled

cells.tense: You are already writing the ending before the rest of it has happened.
cells.ask: Pick one person you've decided about. For one conversation, ask only questions. Don't correct the picture. Let the unfinished version stand until they leave.
cells.core:
You're reading ahead. By the time someone finishes a sentence, you've seen where it goes, and that certainty has started arriving as a verdict. The person in front of you is getting your conclusion instead of your attention.

That's what happens when seeing turns rigid: the pattern stops being something you're in and becomes something you're over. You start managing people for the version of them you've settled on. Some of what you say lands like judgment, even when you mean it as plain sense. The direction you actually want is simple to say and hard to do — choose the next question instead of the next verdict. Being sure out loud is not the same as being right.
cells.sheetLine: You've stopped watching and started pronouncing.

cells.tense: You knew something once and you are still standing at that old door.
cells.ask: Tell one person what you actually notice about a situation you're both in. Just what you see, no conclusion. Say it plainly, without defending it.
cells.core:
There's a way of seeing that used to be yours and it stopped being welcome. Now you wait for the full picture before you say anything, and the full picture doesn't come. So what you've noticed sits there, unspoken, and from the outside it can look like you're not paying attention.

You are. You're just holding it until it's safe enough to hand over, and that day keeps not arriving. What's actually missing isn't more insight. It's the small ordinary presence that lets a partial read be said out loud into a room. The person in front of you doesn't need your conclusion. They need you available, noticing, ready to speak before you've finished seeing.
cells.sheetLine: You're waiting for the whole picture before you say anything.
cells.verb: seeing the whole pattern, from inside it and outside it at once

cells.tense: You are already seeing what's out of proportion here and calling it someone else's call.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've been quietly calling unfair. Say it plainly to the person who can do something about it. Don't argue the case. Just say it and stay in the room.
cells.core:
You can see where the weight is off — who's carrying more, who got less, what isn't adding up — and you've been treating that as something you merely notice. It's not. The read is yours, and you keep handing it off to circumstance.

The line between you and fairness has gone blurry. You describe the imbalance like a fact of the room instead of something you're already measuring. That measurement is yours. Saying so out loud, plainly, without turning it into a fight, is how it comes back to you. The person next to you will feel the difference the moment you stop reporting and start speaking.
cells.sheetLine: You've seen the imbalance. You're calling it nobody's call.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that this person has seen the whole pattern and knows it; the record only supports that recognition is the capacity at issue at this seat, so I will write it as a condition of that capacity, not as proof of history or motive. A reader could reasonably say they don't feel they see the pattern right now, so the ask must be usable even by someone who disagrees with the read. The ask survives being wrong because it is an act of turning the pattern into a fair arrangement with one person, which helps regardless of whether recognition is the issue. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you have a gift for seeing,' which praises my read rather than their life.
